questions.q: Which team owns the schema of the order.placed event?
questions.explain: An event is owned by its producer. Consumers adapt to it, and the producer has to keep old and new consumers working, which is what versions and tolerant readers are for.
options: The orders team, because the event describes the orders service's own facts
The payments team, because payments is the most important consumer
Every consumer jointly, and each must approve every change
Nobody: events are free-form by nature

questions.q: Checkout, the admin panel and the subscriptions service all send a payments.charge command to the payments service's queue. Who should own the command's schema?
questions.explain: A command has many senders and one handler. The handler says what it accepts, exactly like an API provider, and senders adapt to it.
options: Checkout, because it sends the most commands
Payments, because it is the one handler; a command is like an API the handler publishes
Each sender defines its own version of the schema
The message broker's team

questions.q: What does forward compatible mean for a message format?
questions.explain: Forward compatibility is old readers surviving new writers. Backward compatibility is the other direction: new readers reading old data, such as v1 events still in a queue.
options: New code can read data written by old code
Old code can read data written by new code
The format can be sent forward to other services unchanged
The newest version is always used

questions.q: In the ₦NaN bug, orders v2 sent total: { … } and the unchanged payments service read totalKobo. Which property was missing?
questions.explain: Payments was the old reader, orders v2 the new writer. The top-right cell of the compatibility matrix was broken.
options: Backward compatibility: the new orders service could not read old events
Forward compatibility: an old reader met data from a newer writer
Idempotency: the same event was handled twice
Serialization: JSON could not represent the object

questions.q: You must change a field's shape in an event with three consumers. Which release order is safe?
questions.explain: Readers first means that when the new shape appears, everyone already understands it. Old-version support can only go once no old message can exist anywhere. A "coordinated release" never happens atomically across machines.
options: Producer first, then consumers as soon as possible
All four services in one coordinated release at midnight
Consumers first (able to read old and new), then the producer, then remove old-version support later
Consumers first, then remove old-version support, then the producer

questions.q: When can the payments team delete the upcaster that turns order.placed v1 into v2?
questions.explain: v1 messages outlive the code that wrote them. Measure versions in flight and know your retention periods; then deleting old support is a decision backed by evidence. (If you keep an event store forever, the upcaster may indeed be permanent.)
options: As soon as orders v2 is fully deployed
After one successful week in production
When metrics show no v1 messages in flight and the retention of every place a v1 message could still live (queue, dead-letter list, event store) has passed
Never: upcasters must be kept forever

questions.q: Payments v2 (reads v1 and v2) and orders v2 (writes v2) are in production. Which rollback is dangerous?
questions.explain: Rolling back a writer is safe because readers already understand both versions. Rolling back a reader re-creates the ₦NaN situation. Readers must be forward compatible, or at least park what they cannot read.
options: Rolling orders back to v1
Rolling payments back to a v1 build that cannot read v2 events
Both are equally safe
Neither: rollbacks never affect message formats

questions.q: A payments instance receives order.placed with schemaVersion: 3, but its build only knows up to v2. What should it do?
questions.explain: A message from the future means a producer is ahead. Dropping it loses a real order; guessing risks misreading; endless retries burn resources. Parking keeps it safe until the reader can handle it.
options: Drop the message: it cannot be for this build
Parse it as v2 and hope the fields it needs are there
Park it where it can be replayed after an upgrade, and alert
Throw, so the queue retries it forever

questions.q: A producer bug sends a v1 body labelled schemaVersion: 2. In the lesson's reader, what catches it?
questions.explain: The version routes the message; the schema is still the judge. Validating the body against the schema of its claimed version catches producer bugs like this one.
options: The serialization envelope's metadata.version
The upcaster
Parsing the body with the v2 schema, which sends it to the dead-letter list
Nothing: the version number is trusted

questions.q: ShopFlow's message has schemaVersion, and its body envelope from @zudojs/serialization has metadata.version. What is the difference?
questions.explain: Two layers, two versions. The package owns the encoding; you own the payload's shape. Mixing them means a package upgrade could look like a schema change, or the other way round.
options: They are the same number written twice for safety
metadata.version is the serializer's wire format (how values are tagged); schemaVersion is the meaning of the payload, owned by the contract
metadata.version is the producer's release number
schemaVersion is the version of @zudojs/schema

questions.q: Where is a schema that rejects unknown fields (.strict()) a good choice?
questions.explain: Between your own services, readers should tolerate unknown fields so producers can add optional ones. At the public edge you are not expecting newer versions of yourself, so rejecting unknown input is reasonable.
options: In every consumer of an event, to catch changes early
For requests from the public internet, where an unknown field is more likely a typo or an attack
In the previous release's reader, used in forward-compatibility tests
Never

questions.q: During a rolling deploy, an old orders instance reads an order document, changes the address and saves the whole document. The giftMessage added by the new version is gone. What is the best fix?
questions.explain: Stripping is safe for reading and dangerous for read-modify-write. Updating only your own fields, or passing unknown ones through, keeps data you do not understand.
options: Make the schema strict so the old instance refuses the document
Update only the fields you own (or keep unknown fields with passthrough() when you must rewrite the whole document)
Stop doing rolling deploys
Add giftMessage to the old version's schema retroactively

questions.q: The checkout team wants to add "ussd" to the method enum in payment.requested. Which statement is right?
questions.explain: An added enum value is new data for old readers. Map unknown values to an explicit, handled case (like "hold for manual review"), deploy that first, and only then start sending the new value.
options: It is always safe: adding values never breaks anyone
Old readers with an enum schema reject the message, so readers must learn to handle unknown values before the producer sends "ussd"
Readers should treat unknown values as the first known value
Enum changes require deleting the old enum

questions.q: Orders v3 registers a Money transformer and starts sending Money objects with preserveTypes. What does an older reader that never registered Money see?
questions.explain: A reader can only rebuild types it knows. A new tagged type is a breaking change for old readers: register the transformer in readers first, then start sending it.
options: A Money instance, rebuilt automatically
The raw tagged object { $type: "Money", $value: … } without strict, or an InvalidSerializedDataError with strict
A plain number of kobo
undefined

questions.q: Which of these does not belong in a shared contracts package?
questions.explain: A contract is data about data. Behaviour in a shared package forces lock-step upgrades whenever it changes, which recreates the monolith's coupling with extra network hops.
options: The schemas for each version of each event
The TypeScript types inferred from those schemas
Example payloads (fixtures) for every version
A calculateDiscount() function both services use

questions.q: Both services import type OrderPlacedV2 from the contracts package. Why must payments still parse incoming events with the schema?
questions.explain: The type is what you hope arrives. Services deploy independently, so the bytes on the wire may come from a different version of the contracts than the one you compiled with.
options: TypeScript types are slower than schemas
Types disappear at runtime and the producer may run a different build; only a runtime check proves what arrived
Parsing is only needed for events from outside the company
It does not need to: shared types make both sides agree

questions.q: What does consumer-driven contract testing tell the provider that a schema alone does not?
questions.explain: A schema says what may be sent. Consumer expectations say what is used. That turns "is this change safe?" from a guess into a test result with names attached.
options: Whether the provider's code has bugs in its business logic
Which fields and interactions each consumer actually relies on, and so which consumer a change would break
How fast the provider answers
Whether the network between services is reliable

questions.q: What is a provider state such as "order ord_1 is pending with 2 lamps at ₦1,250"?
questions.explain: The consumer names the situation it assumes; the provider's verification code creates that data (here, an order in a map) before calling its real service.
options: The provider's current deployment status
A named setup the provider performs before replaying an interaction, so the expected response is predictable
A state machine inside the orders service
The HTTP status the consumer expects

questions.q: Why did the payments pact use exact(250000) for totalKobo but like("NGN") for currency?
questions.explain: Exact values tied to a state catch semantic changes such as naira instead of kobo. Exact values that do not follow from the state make pacts brittle.
options: Numbers must always be exact and strings never
The total follows from the provider state (2 × ₦1,250), so an exact value catches a change of meaning; other values should only be type-checked so harmless data changes do not break the pact
exact is faster to check
It is a mistake; both should be exact

questions.q: A release changes totalKobo from 250000 to 2500 (naira) without renaming it. Which check fails?
questions.explain: Same name, same type, different meaning. Only a check that knows the expected value for a known situation can catch it.
options: The JSON Schema check: it is an integer, but the wrong integer
A like(250000) matcher
An exact(250000) expectation under a provider state that fixes the order's contents
None: such a change cannot be detected by any test

questions.q: Orders 2.5.0 has been verified against payments 1.9.0. Production runs payments 1.8.0. May orders 2.5.0 be deployed?
questions.explain: can-i-deploy asks about the consumer versions actually in production. A verification against a version nobody runs yet proves nothing about today's traffic.
options: Yes, because it was verified against a newer payments
No, not until it is verified against payments 1.8.0 or payments 1.9.0 is in production
Yes, if the orders team's own unit tests pass
Only during a maintenance window

questions.q: In the consumer test, payments' code ran against a fake orders server that returned only values built from the pact. Why?
questions.explain: The consumer test keeps the pact honest. Without it, a consumer could depend on a field it never declared, and provider verification would miss that dependency.
options: The real orders service is too slow for tests
If payments reads a field it did not declare, the fake returns undefined and the consumer test fails, so the pact really lists everything payments uses
To test the orders service's business logic
Fake servers are required by @zudojs/rpc

questions.q: A week after publishing order.placed v2, you notice couponCode should have been an object. What do you do?
questions.explain: Once a version is published, messages of that shape exist in queues and stores. Changing the schema under them turns valid messages invalid. A fix is always a new version.
options: Edit the v2 schema, since only a week has passed
Publish v3 with the new shape and an upcaster from v2; v2 stays as it was
Delete all v2 events and republish them
Rename the event type to avoid versions

questions.q: Why is a table read directly by two services described as "a contract with no version, no owner and no tests"?
questions.explain: A shared table couples both services to its exact layout. An event or an API puts a versioned, testable contract at the boundary instead.
options: Databases do not support schemas
Any column change by the owning service can break the other service, with nothing in between to version, validate or verify the dependency
Two services reading one table is always too slow
SQL cannot be tested

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: By default @zudojs/schema object schemas strip unknown keys: the parse succeeds and the result contains only the declared fields. That is the tolerant-reader behaviour.
options: true [ 'orderId', 'totalKobo' ]
true [ 'orderId', 'totalKobo', 'couponCode' ]
false [ 'orderId', 'totalKobo' ]
TypeError: Cannot convert undefined or null to object

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: .strict() turns an unknown key into an issue. For a reader between services, that makes every harmless new field a breaking change.
options: false Unknown key: channel
true
false Required field missing: channel
false Expected object, received object

questions.q: An old instance updates the address. What does this print?
questions.explain: The default strips giftMessage, so writing a back would delete it. passthrough() keeps unknown keys, so b still has all three.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A v1 body runs through both steps, 1→2 then 2→3. The v1 step builds a new object, so totalNaira is gone. A v3 body needs no step and comes out unchanged.
options:
{ id: 'ord_1', totalKobo: 250000, currency: 'NGN' }
{ id: 'ord_3', totalKobo: 900, currency: 'GHS' }

{ id: 'ord_1', totalKobo: 250000 }
{ id: 'ord_3', totalKobo: 900, currency: 'GHS' }

{ id: 'ord_1', totalNaira: 2500, totalKobo: 250000, currency: 'NGN' }
{ id: 'ord_3', totalKobo: 900, currency: 'GHS' }

{ id: 'ord_1', totalKobo: 250000, currency: 'NGN' }
{ id: 'ord_3', totalKobo: 900, currency: 'NGN' }

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The old reader returns undefined for the new shape, and Array.prototype.join writes undefined as an empty string, so the line ends with a space. The silent undefined is exactly how the ₦NaN bug started.
options:
old 500
new 500 700

old 500 undefined
new 500 700

old 500 NaN
new 500 700

old 500
new 700 700

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: This build understands wire-format version 1, so an envelope claiming version 2 is refused instead of misread. unwrapEnvelope returns the raw data string; it does not parse it.
options:
InvalidSerializedDataError
{"orderId":"ord_1"}

{"orderId":"ord_1"}
{"orderId":"ord_1"}

InvalidSerializedDataError
{ orderId: 'ord_1' }

TypeError
{"orderId":"ord_1"}

questions.q: A newer producer sent a Money value. What does this older reader print?
questions.explain: Without strict, an unknown tag is left as a plain tagged object, while known tags like Date are rebuilt. The reader gets something it did not expect, silently. Use strict between services to fail loudly instead.
options: Money true
undefined true
Money false
InvalidSerializedDataError

questions.q: Using a small version of the lesson's pact checker, what does this print?
questions.explain: The checker walks into nested expectations, so it reports the missing customer.email with its full path. It only checks declared fields, so the extra note is fine: consumers are tolerant readers.
options: [ '$.customer.email is missing', '$.totalKobo should be number' ]
[ '$.customer.email is missing', '$.totalKobo should be number', '$.note is not allowed' ]
[ '$.totalKobo should be number' ]
[ '$.customer is missing', '$.totalKobo should be number' ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The enum schema rejects the new value outright. The tolerant version accepts any string and maps unknown ones to an explicit "unknown" that the code must handle.
options: false unknown card
true ussd card
false ussd card
false unknown unknown

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: shipping@5 was verified, but production runs shipping@4. email@1 was never verified at all, perhaps because it has no pact yet, which is a finding in itself.
options: wait for shipping@4 and email@1
deploy
wait for shipping@4
wait for email@1

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Old versions are upcast, the current one handled, a version from the future parked for later, and a message this reader should never receive goes to the dead-letter list for a human.
options:
1 upcast, then handle
2 handle
3 parked
dead-letter

1 handle
2 handle
3 parked
dead-letter

1 upcast, then handle
2 handle
3 dead-letter
dead-letter

1 upcast, then handle
2 handle

parked

questions.q: A v2 schema adds a required field. What does this print?
questions.explain: A new required field breaks backward compatibility: stored messages do not have it. Make it optional, or add an upcaster that fills it in.
options: false true
true true
false false
true false

questions.q: Payments v1 formats the amount. What does this print for a v2 event?
questions.explain: undefined / 100 is NaN, and NaN.toFixed(2) is the string "NaN". No exception is thrown, which is why this kind of break slips through.
options: TypeError ₦4800.00
₦undefined ₦4800.00

questions.q: Write readLatest(version, body) for order.placed, where the latest version is 2. Version 1 bodies are { orderId, totalKobo }; version 2 bodies are { orderId, total: { amountMinor, currency } }, and every v1 order was in "NGN". A version above 2 must throw an error with the message parked: v3 (for version 3).
questions.explain: Upcast old versions to one shape so the handler has a single code path, and refuse versions from the future instead of guessing what they mean.

questions.q: Write readMethod(value) that returns "card" or "transfer" for those values and "unknown" for anything else (including non-strings), then route(method) that returns "gateway", "await-transfer" or "manual-review".
questions.explain: A tolerant reader never rejects the whole message for a value it does not know, and never silently treats it as a known value. "Unknown" gets its own, safe handling.
questions.expected:
card -> gateway
transfer -> await-transfer
ussd -> manual-review
42 -> manual-review

questions.q: Print a compatibility line for each reader: its name, then ok or BROKEN for each writer, in order. A reader is broken for a writer when it throws or returns something that is not an integer.
questions.explain: "analytics v1" was written against the new shape only, so it cannot read old events still in the queue: it is not backward compatible. Only a reader that is ok in every column may run while both writers exist.
questions.expected:
payments v1 ok BROKEN
payments v2 ok ok
analytics v1 BROKEN ok

questions.q: Write missingFields(expected, actual). expected is an object whose values are either true (the field must exist) or a nested object of the same kind. Return the paths of missing fields, like "customer.email".
questions.explain: Recursion follows nested expectations. When a whole object is missing, reporting the object itself (not each field inside it) keeps the message short and accurate.

questions.q: Write canIDeploy(candidate, production, verified). It returns "yes" if verified contains candidate|consumer@version for every consumer in production, otherwise "no: " followed by the unverified consumers joined with ", ".
questions.explain: The check is about what runs in production now. A candidate verified against a newer consumer must still wait until that consumer is deployed.

questions.q: Complete outcome(message) using @zudojs/schema. Messages with schemaVersion above 2 are "parked". Version 1 bodies ({ orderId, totalKobo }) are upcast to v2 ({ orderId, total: { amountMinor, currency: "NGN" } }). The result is "handled ORDER_ID" if the v2 schema accepts the body, otherwise "dead-letter".
questions.explain: The version decides the route (park, upcast or handle), and the schema has the last word: the third message claims v2 but carries a v1 body, so it is dead-lettered for a human to inspect.
questions.expected:
handled ord_1
handled ord_2
dead-letter
parked

questions.q: Count the messages in flight by type@vVERSION and print each count in the order first seen, like order.placed@v1: 2. This is the evidence you need before deleting an upcaster.
questions.explain: A Map keeps insertion order, so the report lists keys in the order first seen. In production the same counter is a metric labelled with type and version, watched until the old version reaches zero.

questions.q: Use @zudojs/serialization to send a reminder with a BigInt amount across a "wire". Wrap { orderId: "ord_1", amountKobo: 250000n } with serializeToEnvelope (with preserveTypes), turn the envelope into a JSON string and back, then read it with deserializeFromEnvelope and print the amount's type and the envelope's format and version.
questions.explain: The envelope's metadata tells the reader how to decode the data (format json, wire-format version 1), and preserveTypes brings the BigInt back as a BigInt. The schema version of your own payload is a separate number you add around it.
